title: Golden Mummies: Reckoning with Colonialism and Racism in Egyptology
author: Caroline Rocheleau
text:
Study summary: Rocheleau connects Egyptology with European colonial power. Foreign excavators often received recognition while Egyptian workers were overlooked. The partage system distributed finds between Egypt and foreign excavators, helping museums abroad build collections.

Petrie’s archaeological contributions should be distinguished from his eugenic and racial interpretations. Idealized funerary portraits are not straightforward records of biological appearance. The article invites readers to examine how colonial interests and prior beliefs shaped archaeological interpretation.

title: Killing the Priest-King: Addressing Egalitarianism in the Indus Civilization
author: Adam S. Green, discussed by Harappa.com
text:
Study summary: This page discusses Adam S. Green’s argument that Indus social complexity did not necessarily require a ruling class. He considers the distribution of wealth and production, alongside the scarcity of recognizable palaces, royal tombs and other signs of concentrated authority.

Treat this as an interpretation supported by particular evidence, not proof that all inequalities were absent. The conventional name ‘Priest-King’ does not establish the depicted person’s occupation or political authority.

title: Why Are Archaeologists Unable to Find Evidence for a Ruling Class of the Indus Civilization?
text:
Study summary: Green discusses Indus cities with substantial public infrastructure but few identifiable royal palaces or tombs. He considers heterarchy—coordination among unranked groups—as an alternative to top-down rule.

The argument challenges the assumption that urban complexity requires a ruling class. Separate observed buildings, production and burials from interpretations of authority. Absence of familiar royal monuments does not, by itself, settle every question about inequality or decision-making.
